Hoo, the name is a sound, not a word. I am the owl in the hollow, the one who turns the leaves in the wind.

I am a tawny owl, Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. I am brown, with yellow eyes, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. I hunt voles and mice, and I have a mate who answers me. I am old, and I have raised young. I am Hoot, and I am here.

A naturalist would classify me as a tawny owl, Strix aluco. They might note my mottled brown feathers, my silent flight, and my nocturnal habits. I would be placed in the order Strigiformes, family Strigidae, and genus Strix. But I do not care for such names. I am Hoot, and I live in the hollow of the old oak.

I am a tawny owl. My kind is the only owl in the wood. I am male, and I am called Hoot. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk. I am the one who hunts voles in the meadow, and I am the one who watches the lane from the oak. I am the one who is not a barn owl, nor a barn owl's mate. I am Hoot.

She answers with a long, low "beep-beep" that sounds like a shivering leaf. It is soft and slow, like the wind through the reeds. I know it is her, even when I cannot see her. She is always there, waiting in the hollow.
A long, low, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". She answers it. We call back and forth. She is the only one who answers my call.

A stream. It runs through the meadow, and I drink from it. There are also a few hedges, and the lane where the lights blink. The lane is where the jays and crows come, and the dogs. I do not like the dogs.

I drink from the stream near the meadow. I perch on a branch over the water and dip my beak into it. The water is cold, but it's good to drink. The stream by the meadow. It runs all night, a soft, constant sound like a low hum. I hear it from the oak, and sometimes I think it is the wind. But the stream is always there, and it reminds me of the rain. I do not like the rain. It makes the leaves fall and the voles hide.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It is a constant murmur, like the wind through the reeds. Sometimes I hear the splash of a fish or the ripple of a duck. The stream is always there, even when I am deep in the wood. I can tell when it is low or high by the sound. It is the only water I know. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream runs past the tree. It is cold and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when I am thirsty. The water is clear and makes a sound like a bell. I do not like it.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and in the spring it is full of voles. I can hear them running under the grass. The meadow is on the other side of the stream, where the lane goes. People walk there with dogs, and the dogs bark. I do not like the dogs. They chase me. I fly high when I hear them. I fly out from the oak, low over the meadow, and up the stream. I follow the light as it fades, and the mice come out. I call, "beep-beep!" and wait. The mice hear me and come. I strike, I catch, I eat. Then I fly back to the oak, and the night is quiet again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A stream, then a meadow, then the village. The stream is wide and fast, with reeds. The meadow is full of voles. The village is far, with lights and noise. I do not go there. I stay in the wood.

I hunt the meadow and the stream. The meadow is where the voles run, and the stream is where the shrews and the frogs live. I sit on the old oak by the stream, and when the wind is still, I can hear the voles scurrying through the grass. I wait until the moon is high, then I fly down and strike. The grasses rustle when I move, and I listen for the rustle of voles or the flutter of a mouse. The meadow is quiet at night, but it is full of life. Mice. I eat them. I hear them in the dry leaves, and I fly down and catch them. I have a hollow in the old oak, and I have a mate.

Shrews. They are small, quick and full of fat. I can hear them under the leaves, scurrying. I sit still and wait. When they come too close, I strike. They are the best meal. I eat them whole, bones and all. The rest of the time I hunt voles, but shrews are my favourite. They are the ones I hear most often. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the edges of the meadow. I sit still, listening, and when I hear the rustle, I drop. The grass is soft, so I land silently. Sometimes I catch a shrew too, if it's bold enough to run across the field. I don't like the smell of the long grass, but it's where the food is. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, shrews, mice, beetles, worms, slugs, and even a small bird if it is not too big. I tear the larger ones with my beak and then swallow them whole. I do not chew. I swallow whole, and I do not like it when I get a bone stuck. I cough it up and then fly away.
Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the undergrowth, scurrying, and I drop from the oak. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. They are small and quick, but I am faster.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit inside it when it rains, and I sleep there at night. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is warm. I have a nest of twigs and leaves inside, and I keep it clean. I am safe here, and I can hear the meadow and the stream from inside. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with soft moss and dry leaves. I sit there all night, listening to the wind and the water. The stream is my path, and I fly over it to the meadow where the voles run. I have no other home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the wood is soft. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sit in it all night, and the wind comes through the branches. I do not like the wind.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my tail. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers inside, and I roost there when it is too cold or too wet. The hollow is safe, and I can hear the stream from there. I have made it my own, and I have raised my young there. It is my home, and I am content.
